teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Crystal size as a record of cooling rate is the most diagnostic formation-property link in the rock cycle. Students who learn it as a memorised fact cannot apply the reasoning to novel samples or explain why the property exists.
teacher_glossary.response: Ask: 'If crystals grow over time, what happens if the rock cools slowly? What if it cools fast?' Students derive the crystal size rule from the mechanism — slower cooling = more time = larger crystals. Then test: classify an unknown igneous sample using crystal size alone.

teacher_glossary.definition: Molten rock located beneath Earth's surface. When magma cools underground, it forms intrusive igneous rock with large crystals. When magma reaches the surface (becoming lava), it forms extrusive igneous rock with small crystals. Magma is produced at divergent boundaries and subduction zones through plate tectonic processes.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students use magma and lava interchangeably — miss that the distinction (underground vs surface) determines the cooling environment and therefore the crystal size of the resulting rock.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If magma and lava are the same, the intrusive/extrusive distinction collapses and students cannot explain why granite and basalt have different crystal sizes despite both forming from molten rock.
teacher_glossary.response: Define by location: magma = underground; lava = same material, at the surface. Then connect: underground = insulated = slow cooling = large crystals; surface = exposed = fast cooling = small crystals.

teacher_glossary.definition: Molten rock that has reached Earth's surface through volcanic eruptions. Lava is the same material as magma but at the surface, where it cools rapidly. This rapid cooling produces extrusive igneous rock with small crystals or glassy texture.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students use lava and magma interchangeably — miss that the surface location determines rapid cooling and therefore small crystal size.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The magma/lava distinction is the same as the intrusive/extrusive distinction. Conflating them prevents students from using location to predict crystal size and rock type.
teacher_glossary.response: Ask: 'Is it underground or at the surface?' Underground = magma = slow cooling = big crystals. Surface = lava = fast cooling = small crystals. Location determines everything.

teacher_glossary.definition: Igneous rock that formed from magma cooling slowly underground, surrounded by insulating rock. Slow cooling allows time for large crystal growth. Granite is the most common example. Intrusive igneous bodies are exposed at the surface only after the overlying rock is removed by weathering and erosion over geological time.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students cannot explain why intrusive rock is found at the surface if it formed underground — miss that millions of years of erosion can expose deeply buried rock.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If students cannot explain surface exposure of intrusive rock, the connection between deep formation and surface observation is broken. This reasoning connects to geological timescale understanding and the rock cycle's uplift pathway.
teacher_glossary.response: Ask: 'Granite formed kilometres underground. How is it at the surface now?' The answer — millions of years of erosion removed the rock above — connects formation depth to geological timescale.

sub_terms.definition: A common intrusive igneous rock with large, visible crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica, formed from magma cooling slowly deep underground.

teacher_glossary.definition: Igneous rock that formed from lava cooling rapidly at Earth's surface. Rapid cooling allows little time for crystal growth, producing fine-grained or glassy texture. Basalt and obsidian are common examples. Extrusive igneous activity occurs at divergent boundaries and volcanic arcs.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think all igneous rock comes from dramatic volcanic eruptions — miss that most extrusive rock forms from less dramatic lava flows, and that some volcanic glass (obsidian) cooled so fast that no crystals formed at all.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If igneous formation is only explosive eruption, students have a narrow view of where and how extrusive rock forms. The continuum from fine-grained basalt to glassy obsidian demonstrates how cooling rate determines texture across a range.
teacher_glossary.response: Present basalt (fine crystals) and obsidian (no crystals) side by side. Both are extrusive — ask what the difference in texture tells you about their cooling rates. The comparison extends the cooling-rate reasoning within the extrusive category.

sub_terms.definition: A common extrusive igneous rock with fine-grained crystals, formed from lava cooling rapidly at Earth's surface. The most common rock on the ocean floor.
A volcanic glass formed when lava cools so rapidly that no crystals have time to form, producing a smooth, glassy texture.

teacher_glossary.definition: The size of mineral crystals in an igneous rock, determined by the cooling rate of the magma or lava from which it formed. Slow cooling underground produces large, visible crystals; rapid cooling at the surface produces small crystals or no crystals (glassy texture). Crystal size is the most diagnostic formation-property link in igneous rock classification — it directly records cooling history.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students memorise crystal size associations (granite = big, basalt = small) without understanding the cooling-rate mechanism that produces the difference.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Memorised associations fail when students encounter unfamiliar samples. The cooling-rate mechanism is a transferable reasoning tool — students who understand it can classify any igneous rock from crystal size alone and explain why.
teacher_glossary.response: Conduct a crystallisation experiment: dissolve salt or alum and cool one sample rapidly (ice bath) and another slowly (insulated container). Compare the crystal sizes produced. The experiment makes the mechanism observable.

sub_terms.definition: The speed at which molten rock loses heat and solidifies. Determined by location — underground (slow, insulated) versus surface (fast, exposed to air/water).
The process by which minerals form ordered crystal structures as molten rock cools and solidifies.

teacher_glossary.definition: Rock formed when any pre-existing rock (sedimentary, igneous or metamorphic) is subjected to intense heat and pressure without melting, causing minerals to recrystallise and realign. Observable properties include banding or foliation (minerals compressed and reoriented), increased density and hardness relative to the parent rock. Metamorphic conditions occur at subduction zones and during mountain building.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think metamorphic rock forms by melting and re-solidifying — confuse it with igneous formation. The defining feature of metamorphism is transformation without melting.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If metamorphism involves melting, it is just igneous formation by another name. The without-melting criterion is what makes metamorphic rock a distinct category — recrystallisation under heat and pressure produces different properties from cooling from a melt.
teacher_glossary.response: Use the analogy of pressing and heating clay versus melting and re-casting metal. Both change the material, but the processes and results are fundamentally different. Ask: 'If the rock melted, what would it be called instead?'

sub_terms.definition: The intensity of heat and pressure a rock experienced during metamorphism. Higher grade produces more dramatic changes — shale → slate (low grade) → schist (high grade).

teacher_glossary.definition: The process by which minerals in a rock are reorganised into new crystal structures under heat and pressure, without the rock melting. Recrystallisation produces denser, harder rock with realigned mineral grains. It is the defining process of metamorphism — distinguishing it from igneous formation where rock melts and recrystallises from a liquid.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse recrystallisation with crystallisation from a melt — miss that recrystallisation occurs in the solid state under pressure, not from cooling liquid.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If recrystallisation is the same as crystallisation from a melt, the distinction between metamorphic and igneous rock collapses. The solid-state transformation is the key difference.
teacher_glossary.response: Compare: crystallisation = crystals forming as liquid cools (igneous); recrystallisation = existing crystals reorganising under pressure without melting (metamorphic). The liquid-vs-solid distinction is the defining difference.

teacher_glossary.definition: The parallel alignment of mineral grains in metamorphic rock, produced by directional pressure during metamorphism. Flat or elongated minerals are compressed and rotated perpendicular to the direction of pressure, creating visible bands or layers. Foliation is a diagnostic property of metamorphic rocks — its presence indicates the rock has been subjected to directed pressure.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse metamorphic banding with sedimentary layering — both produce visible bands but through entirely different mechanisms.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Sedimentary layers record sequential deposition; metamorphic bands record directional pressure. If the two are confused, students cannot use banding to identify rock type or infer formation conditions.
teacher_glossary.response: Compare a layered sedimentary rock and a foliated metamorphic rock. Ask: 'How did each set of bands form?' Sedimentary = deposited in layers over time; metamorphic = minerals squashed and realigned by pressure. The mechanism is different even though the appearance is similar.

teacher_glossary.definition: The pre-existing rock from which a metamorphic rock formed. Parent rock determines what minerals are available for recrystallisation, which determines the metamorphic product: shale → slate; limestone → marble; sandstone → quartzite. Identifying parent-product pairs connects observable metamorphic properties to formation history.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think metamorphism creates entirely new minerals from nothing — miss that the minerals in metamorphic rock are reorganised from the parent rock's existing minerals.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If metamorphism creates new minerals from nothing, students cannot predict what metamorphic rock will form from a given parent. The parent → product relationship is the reasoning tool for interpreting metamorphic formation history.
teacher_glossary.response: Present parent-product pairs (shale → slate, limestone → marble) and ask what stayed the same and what changed. The minerals are the same — their arrangement changed. This makes metamorphism a reorganisation, not a creation.

teacher_glossary.definition: The continuous set of interconnected processes by which rocks are transformed between sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic types over geological time. Any rock type can become any other — sedimentary can be buried and metamorphosed, metamorphic can melt and form igneous, igneous can weather to sediment. The rock cycle is driven by plate tectonics (providing heat, pressure and uplift) and surface processes (weathering and erosion). No rock is permanent.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think the rock cycle is a fixed sequence (sedimentary → metamorphic → igneous → sedimentary) rather than a web of possible pathways — miss that any rock type can transform into any other.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If the rock cycle is a fixed sequence, students cannot trace alternative pathways (e.g. igneous → sedimentary directly, skipping metamorphic) or understand that rocks can cycle through the same type repeatedly. The web model is essential for understanding Earth as a dynamic system.
teacher_glossary.response: Ask students to trace three different pathways through the rock cycle, starting from the same rock. Each pathway should skip at least one rock type. The variety of possible routes makes the web structure visible.

teacher_glossary.definition: The tectonic process that raises rock formed deep underground to Earth's surface, where it is exposed to weathering and erosion. Uplift occurs at convergent boundaries (mountain building) and through isostatic rebound. Without uplift, deeply buried rocks would never re-enter the surface part of the rock cycle. Uplift is what makes the rock cycle a cycle rather than a one-way journey downward.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students do not consider how deep rocks reach the surface — the connection between tectonic uplift and rock exposure is missed.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Without uplift, the rock cycle has no return path from depth to surface. Students who miss uplift cannot explain how metamorphic or intrusive igneous rocks — formed kilometres underground — end up at the surface where we can observe them.
teacher_glossary.response: Ask: 'Granite formed kilometres underground. Slate formed under intense pressure deep in the crust. How are both now at the surface?' The answer — tectonic uplift raised them, then erosion exposed them — completes the cycle.

teacher_glossary.definition: The immense time periods over which rock cycle processes operate — typically thousands to hundreds of millions of years. Surface processes (weathering, erosion) operate over thousands to millions of years; deep processes (metamorphism, melting, burial) operate over tens to hundreds of millions of years. Understanding geological timescale is essential for appreciating why rock appears permanent in human experience but is temporary in Earth's history.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students underestimate geological timescales — they think rock cycle processes take hundreds or thousands of years rather than millions, or cannot conceptualise the difference between human and geological time.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If timescales are underestimated, students cannot understand why rocks appear permanent (human timescale) yet are temporary (geological timescale). This dual perspective is what makes the rock cycle conceptually challenging — 'no rock is permanent' requires geological-scale thinking.
teacher_glossary.response: Use a proportional timeline: if Earth's history is one year, human civilisation is the last few seconds of December 31st. Rock cycle processes that seem impossibly slow are fast on this scale. The proportion makes geological time tangible.

teacher_glossary.definition: A classification tool that uses a series of paired questions with two possible answers at each step to identify a specimen. In rock identification, dichotomous keys use observable properties — crystal size, grain shape, banding, fossil presence — to classify samples as sedimentary, igneous or metamorphic and identify specific rock types. Each question narrows the possibilities by half.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students follow the key mechanically without understanding why each question discriminates — they get answers without understanding the property-based reasoning behind each branch.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If students follow keys mechanically, they cannot construct their own keys, adapt when a key does not cover their sample, or transfer the classification reasoning to new contexts. The key is a tool for applying formation-property reasoning, not a substitute for it.
teacher_glossary.response: Ask students to explain why each question in the key was chosen — what property does it test and what formation information does that property reveal? Then ask them to construct a key for a different set of samples.

teacher_glossary.definition: Energy associated with active motion or activity — at the level of objects, particles or waves. Kinetic energy unifies energy forms students have encountered in prior years (sound, heat, light, electrical, movement) under one classification category. The shared characteristic is that something is actively happening — particles vibrating, objects moving, waves propagating, charges flowing.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students treat kinetic energy as only movement energy (objects in motion) — miss that thermal, sound, light and electrical energy are all kinetic because they involve active processes at the particle or wave level.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If kinetic energy is only movement, the classification framework collapses — students cannot explain why heat is kinetic (particles vibrating) or why light is kinetic (waves propagating). The unifying principle is activity, not just visible motion.
teacher_glossary.response: For each kinetic type, ask 'What is actively happening?' Movement = object moving. Thermal = particles vibrating. Sound = air molecules vibrating. Light = waves propagating. Electrical = charges flowing. The active-process test makes the category coherent.

sub_terms.definition: Kinetic energy carried by vibrating particles — a sound wave is a pressure wave of particle vibration moving through a medium.
Kinetic energy carried by electromagnetic waves. Also called radiant energy.
Kinetic energy associated with the flow of electric charges through a conductor.
Kinetic energy of a moving object — the most intuitive kinetic form.

teacher_glossary.definition: The kinetic energy of particles vibrating and moving within a substance. Thermal energy is proportional to temperature — faster particle motion means higher temperature. At Year 8, it is critical that students understand thermal energy as kinetic (active particle motion) rather than potential (stored). Thermal energy is also the most common by-product of energy transformations, making it central to N4–N6.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think heat energy is stored in hot objects like a battery stores energy — they classify thermal energy as potential rather than kinetic.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If thermal energy is potential, the entire kinetic/potential classification breaks. More importantly, by-product heat in transformations (N4) cannot be understood as active energy dissipating into the surroundings — it would be treated as stored energy, which prevents correct efficiency analysis in Year 9.
teacher_glossary.response: Ask: 'Is anything actively happening in a hot object?' Yes — particles are vibrating faster. That active vibration IS the thermal energy. Compare to a stretched spring (potential — nothing is happening yet, but it could). The activity test resolves the classification.

teacher_glossary.definition: Energy stored in an object due to its position, composition or state of deformation — not currently active, but capable of being released. The three main forms at Year 8 are chemical (energy stored in molecular bonds — food, fuel, batteries), gravitational (energy due to height above a reference point) and elastic (energy stored in stretched or compressed materials). Potential energy becomes kinetic when the stored condition changes.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students cannot identify potential energy because it is invisible — if nothing is visibly happening, they think there is no energy present.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If potential energy is invisible and therefore non-existent, students cannot trace the energy present before a transformation begins. A ball at the top of a ramp, food before digestion, a stretched rubber band — all have energy that will convert to kinetic. Missing the 'before' state makes energy tracing in N5 incomplete.
teacher_glossary.response: Present 'before and after' scenarios: ball at top of ramp → ball rolling; food → body moving; stretched rubber band → band snapping. Ask where the kinetic energy came from. The answer forces recognition of the stored energy present before the change.

sub_terms.definition: Energy stored in the bonds between atoms in molecules. Released during chemical reactions — combustion, digestion, battery discharge.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students do not recognise food, fuel or batteries as containing energy because nothing is visibly happening — they reserve 'energy' for moving or hot objects.
sub_terms.response: Ask: 'Where does the energy come from when you run after eating? It was stored in the food — in molecular bonds. Where does torch light come from? Energy stored in the battery.' The before-action source makes chemical PE concrete.

sub_terms.definition: Energy stored due to an object's height above a reference point. The higher the object, the more gravitational potential energy it has.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think gravitational potential energy only matters at extreme heights — miss that any height above a reference point stores GPE, including a book on a desk.
sub_terms.response: Drop a book from desk height and from hand height. Both had GPE — the desk drop just had more. Ask: 'At what height does GPE become zero?' Only at the reference point — the concept is continuous, not threshold-based.

sub_terms.definition: Energy stored in a stretched, compressed or deformed material. Released when the material returns to its original shape.

teacher_glossary.definition: Energy moving from one object or location to another without changing type. The energy type is preserved but its location changes — heat flows from a hot object to a cold one (thermal → thermal), a moving ball hits a stationary ball (kinetic → kinetic), sound travels from speaker to ear (sound → sound). Transfer is distinguished from transformation by the preservation of energy type.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse transfer with transformation — they treat any energy change as a transformation, missing that transfer preserves the energy type while only changing location.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If transfer and transformation are conflated, students cannot correctly identify which steps in a multi-step system change energy type (transformation) and which merely move it (transfer). This distinction is essential for constructing accurate flow diagrams in N6.
teacher_glossary.response: Present two events: heat flowing from a hot mug to a cold hand (same type, different location = transfer) and striking a match (chemical → thermal + light = transformation). Ask students to identify the difference. The contrast is the teaching tool.

teacher_glossary.definition: Energy changing from one type to another. In every transformation, the input energy type differs from the output energy type — chemical → kinetic (combustion), electrical → light (light bulb), gravitational potential → kinetic (falling object). Almost every transformation produces by-product heat alongside the useful output. Identifying both useful output and by-product is essential for complete energy analysis.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students identify the useful output of a transformation but omit by-product heat — the analysis is systematically incomplete.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: By-product heat is the conceptual foundation of efficiency analysis in AC9S9U05. Students who do not identify heat as a by-product of every transformation produce systematically incomplete energy analyses and cannot construct accurate Sankey diagrams or calculate efficiency.
teacher_glossary.response: For every transformation, require students to identify ALL outputs — useful AND by-product. Use the sentence frame: '___ energy → ___ energy (useful) + ___ energy (by-product).' The frame forces completeness.

sub_terms.definition: A chemical reaction in which a fuel reacts with oxygen, releasing thermal and light energy. A common example of chemical potential energy transforming to kinetic energy.

teacher_glossary.definition: Thermal energy produced as an unwanted output in almost every energy transformation. By-product heat is not lost — energy is conserved — but it is not the useful output and typically dissipates into the surroundings. The proportion of energy that becomes by-product heat rather than useful output is what efficiency measures. Sound and friction heat are also common by-products.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think by-product heat means energy is destroyed or lost — miss that it is conserved but not useful.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If by-product heat is 'lost,' energy conservation appears violated. Understanding that the energy still exists but is no longer useful is the conceptual prerequisite for efficiency: efficiency measures how much energy ended up as useful output versus how much became unusable by-product.
teacher_glossary.response: Ask: 'When a light bulb gets hot, where did the heat energy come from? Did any energy disappear?' The answer — electrical energy became light (useful) AND heat (by-product), nothing disappeared — makes conservation and by-product concrete simultaneously.

sub_terms.definition: The energy form that the system is designed to produce — light from a lamp, movement from a motor, sound from a speaker. Distinguished from by-product energy that is produced but not intended.

teacher_glossary.definition: The principle that energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred or transformed. In any energy event, the total energy after equals the total energy before. Energy that appears to be 'lost' has been transformed into by-product heat or other forms that dissipate into the environment. At Year 8, conservation is introduced qualitatively through by-product identification; quantitative efficiency calculations are developed in AC9S9U05.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students accept energy conservation as a rule but apply it inconsistently — they say 'energy is conserved' while also saying by-product heat is 'wasted' or 'lost,' revealing a surface-level understanding.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If conservation is a stated rule rather than a deeply held principle, students will produce analyses that violate it without noticing — missing by-product outputs, or claiming energy disappears. Robust conservation understanding is the foundation of all energy analysis.
teacher_glossary.response: Present a transformation where the useful output seems less than the input (e.g. a car engine). Ask: 'Where did the rest go?' Students must account for ALL output energy to match the input. The accounting exercise makes conservation operational rather than declarative.

teacher_glossary.definition: The analytical skill of following energy through a multi-step system, naming the energy type at each stage and identifying all transfers, transformations and by-product outputs along the way. Energy tracing is the prerequisite skill for flow diagram construction (N6) and efficiency analysis (AC9S9U05). A complete trace accounts for all energy at every stage — no energy appears from nowhere or disappears.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students can identify the start and end energy types but skip intermediate steps — the trace jumps from input to output without accounting for the stages between.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If intermediate steps are skipped, by-product outputs at each stage are missed. A roller coaster trace that goes 'gravitational → kinetic' misses the heat and sound by-products at every conversion. Incomplete traces produce incomplete flow diagrams and inaccurate efficiency calculations.
teacher_glossary.response: Require stage-by-stage tracing: 'At this point, what type of energy is present? What happens next? What type is it now? What by-products were produced?' The step-by-step method prevents skipping.

teacher_glossary.definition: A visual representation of energy moving through a system, using arrows and labels to show the energy type at each stage, all transfers and transformations, and all by-product outputs. Flow diagrams must account for all energy at every transformation — missing by-product arrows is the most common error. Flow diagrams are the representational foundation for Sankey diagrams and efficiency analysis in AC9S9U05.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students construct flow diagrams that show only the useful output pathway — by-product heat arrows are missing from transformation stages, producing an incomplete diagram that appears to violate energy conservation.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Flow diagrams with missing by-products are systematically wrong — they imply energy disappears at each transformation. This error propagates directly into AC9S9U05's Sankey diagrams and efficiency calculations, where every output must be accounted for.
teacher_glossary.response: After students construct a flow diagram, ask: 'Does the total energy leaving each stage equal the energy entering it?' If not, find the missing arrows. By-product heat at each transformation stage is the most commonly missing component.

teacher_glossary.definition: The smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity. At Year 8, the key conceptual move is identifying atoms as the particles in the prior particle model (AC9S7U05) — the undifferentiated particles students already know are now given identity (type). Atoms of the same element are identical; atoms of different elements differ. This is a model — atoms have internal structure, introduced at Year 9 (AC9S9U06).
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think atoms and particles are different things — they maintain two separate mental models rather than understanding that atoms ARE the particles from the particle model.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If atoms and particles are separate concepts, students have a particle model with no identity and an atom concept with no physical model. Connecting the two — 'those particles you know about are atoms, and atoms have type' — is the upgrade that makes element/compound/mixture classification possible.
teacher_glossary.response: Start from the particle model diagrams students already know. Point to a particle and say: 'This is an atom. Now we are adding one new thing — atoms have type.' The upgrade framing prevents fragmentation.

teacher_glossary.definition: The identity of an atom that determines which element it belongs to. All atoms of the same element are the same type; atoms of different elements are different types. There are approximately 118 known atom types, each corresponding to an element. Atom type is the conceptual extension that transforms the Year 7 particle model from undifferentiated particles into particles with identity.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students treat all atoms as identical — the undifferentiated particle model persists even after atom type is introduced.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If all atoms are identical, elements cannot be defined by atom type, compounds cannot be understood as different atom types combined, and the element/compound/mixture classification has no foundation. Atom type is the hinge concept for the entire standard.
teacher_glossary.response: Use coloured particle diagrams where each colour represents a different atom type. Ask: 'What makes oxygen different from carbon?' The answer — different atom type — must be available before element and compound definitions can work.

teacher_glossary.definition: The scientific model describing matter as composed of particles with specific arrangement, motion and attraction forces. At Year 8, the particle model is upgraded — the previously undifferentiated particles are now identified as atoms with type. The model is not replaced; it is extended. At this level, atoms are treated as indivisible units — internal structure (protons, neutrons, electrons) is introduced at Year 9.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think the Year 8 model replaces the Year 7 model rather than extending it — they lose the particle arrangement and motion concepts when atom type is added.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If the models are separate, students cannot use particle arrangement (from Year 7) to explain element/compound/mixture differences (Year 8). The upgrade must preserve prior knowledge while adding the new atom-type layer.
teacher_glossary.response: Explicitly frame the Year 8 addition: 'Everything you know about particles — arrangement, motion, attraction — still applies. We are adding one thing: particles have type.' Show the same particle diagrams from Year 7 with atom-type colour added.

teacher_glossary.definition: A pure substance consisting of only one type of atom. Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means. Each element has a unique symbol (1–2 letters, first capitalised) standardised internationally and located on the periodic table. There are approximately 118 known elements. Element identity is determined by atom type — carbon is carbon because all its atoms are carbon atoms.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think elements are rare, laboratory-only substances — miss that common materials (oxygen in air, carbon in pencils, iron in nails) are elements or contain elements.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If elements are abstract laboratory concepts, students cannot connect the classification system to everyday experience. Recognising common materials as elements or compounds of elements grounds the abstraction in familiar reality.
teacher_glossary.response: Present everyday objects and ask students to identify which are elements (aluminium foil, copper wire, gold ring) and which are compounds. The familiar examples make elements concrete rather than abstract.

teacher_glossary.definition: A one- or two-letter abbreviation representing an element, standardised internationally. The first letter is always capitalised; the second (if present) is always lowercase. Symbols are derived from element names, sometimes from Latin (Fe for iron/ferrum, Au for gold/aurum). Chemical symbols are the building blocks of chemical formulas — students must be able to read and write them fluently.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students write chemical symbols incorrectly — capitalising both letters (CO for cobalt instead of Co) or using incorrect abbreviations — leading to confusion between elements and compounds.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: CO means carbon monoxide (a compound); Co means cobalt (an element). Symbol errors produce meaning errors. Fluent symbol use is a prerequisite for reading and writing chemical formulas.
teacher_glossary.response: Practice the capitalisation rule with tricky examples: Co vs CO, NO vs No. Ask what each represents. The error-prone pairs make the convention meaningful rather than arbitrary.

teacher_glossary.definition: A systematic arrangement of all known elements, organised by atomic number (number of protons). Elements in the same column (group) share similar chemical properties. At Year 8, the periodic table is primarily a reference tool — students use it to locate element names and symbols, and to recognise that element properties vary systematically. The arrangement principle (atomic number) is developed further at Year 9.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students see the periodic table as a chart to memorise rather than a tool to read — they try to memorise symbols instead of learning to look them up efficiently.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The periodic table is a reference tool, not a memorisation test. Students who try to memorise it rather than use it cannot locate unfamiliar elements and miss the systematic property patterns that make the table meaningful.
teacher_glossary.response: Set tasks that require looking up unfamiliar elements: 'What is the symbol for tungsten? What group is selenium in?' The practice builds fluency with the table as a tool rather than a test.

teacher_glossary.definition: A substance containing two or more different atom types chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. Compounds have properties that are different from their constituent elements — the properties emerge from the chemical combination, not the components. NaCl (table salt) is edible; Na (sodium) is dangerously reactive and Cl₂ (chlorine) is toxic. Chemical combination is permanent under normal conditions — separating a compound requires a chemical reaction, not physical separation.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students conflate compounds with mixtures — treat both as 'different atoms together' without distinguishing chemical bonding from physical mixing.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The compound/mixture distinction is the conceptual boundary between chemical and physical combination. Students who conflate them cannot understand why chemical reactions produce genuinely new substances (AC9S8U07) or apply conservation of mass in reactions (AC9S9U07).
teacher_glossary.response: Compare NaCl properties to Na and Cl₂ properties. Ask: 'Is salt anything like a reactive metal or a toxic gas?' The dramatic property change makes chemical combination concrete — mixing does not produce new properties, but chemical combination does.

teacher_glossary.definition: A compact representation of a compound showing which atom types are present and their ratio, using element symbols and subscript numbers. H₂O means two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom per molecule; CO₂ means one carbon and two oxygen atoms. Formulas convey composition (atom types and ratios) but not spatial arrangement — structural formulas and 3D models are needed for that.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students cannot read subscript numbers — they treat H₂O as 'H, 2, O' rather than understanding that the subscript applies to the element immediately before it.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If subscripts cannot be read, students cannot determine atom ratios, cannot balance equations in Year 9, and cannot compare formulas. Formula literacy is the gateway to chemical notation.
teacher_glossary.response: Practice reading formulas aloud: 'H₂O means two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.' Then reverse: 'A molecule with one carbon and two oxygen atoms — write the formula.' Both directions build fluency.

sub_terms.definition: A small number written below and to the right of an element symbol in a chemical formula, indicating the number of atoms of that element. No subscript means one atom.
The constant proportion of atom types in a compound — water is always H₂O (2:1 hydrogen to oxygen), never H₃O or HO. This distinguishes compounds from mixtures, which have variable composition.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students can read the formula H₂O but do not understand that the 2:1 ratio is invariant — they think you could have 'extra hydrogen' water, treating the ratio as a description rather than a defining constraint.
sub_terms.response: Ask: 'Can you make water with three hydrogen atoms instead of two?' No — that would be a different substance. The fixed ratio IS what makes it water. Compare with salt water, where you can add more salt without creating a new substance.

teacher_glossary.definition: The strong attraction holding atoms together in a compound. Chemical bonds are what make compounds stable and give them properties different from their constituent elements. At Year 8, bonds are introduced as the mechanism of chemical combination — the detailed nature of bonding (ionic, covalent) is developed at Year 9. Breaking bonds requires energy; this connects to exothermic/endothermic concepts in AC9S8U07.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think chemical bonds are physical connections like glue or rope — miss that bonds are forces of attraction between atoms, not material links.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If bonds are physical links, students cannot understand why bond breaking requires energy, why compounds have new properties, or how bonds form and break during chemical reactions. The force-of-attraction model is essential for Year 9 chemistry.
teacher_glossary.response: Use magnets as an analogy: the attraction holds them together, but there is no physical thread between them. Ask what happens when you pull magnets apart — you need to do work against the attraction. Chemical bonds work similarly.

teacher_glossary.definition: A combination of two or more substances that are physically combined but not chemically bonded. Components of a mixture retain their individual properties and can be separated by physical means (filtration, evaporation, distillation). Mixtures have variable composition — unlike compounds, the proportions of components can vary. Connects to AC9S7U06's separation techniques.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think all combinations are compounds — miss that mixing is reversible by physical means because no new substance is formed.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If all combinations are compounds, physical separation techniques (AC9S7U06) should not work. The retained-properties, variable-composition, physically-separable criteria are what distinguish mixtures from compounds and explain why separation works.
teacher_glossary.response: Mix salt and sand together. Ask: 'Has a new substance been formed? Can you get the salt and sand back?' Dissolving in water and filtering separates them — the components retained their properties throughout.

sub_terms.definition: The property of mixtures having no fixed ratio of components — you can add more salt to salt water and it is still salt water, unlike compounds which have fixed ratios.
Methods that separate mixture components using physical properties (boiling point, solubility, particle size) rather than chemical reactions. Connects to AC9S7U06.

teacher_glossary.definition: A mixture in which one substance (the solute) is dissolved in another (the solvent), forming a uniform, transparent mixture. The solute particles are evenly distributed among solvent particles at the molecular level. Solutions cannot be separated by filtering because the solute particles are too small — evaporation or distillation is required.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think dissolving is a chemical change because the solid 'disappears' — miss that the solute particles are still present, just dispersed among solvent particles.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If dissolving is a chemical change, salt water is a compound rather than a mixture. This error collapses the compound/mixture distinction and contradicts the separation evidence (evaporating salt water recovers the salt).
teacher_glossary.response: Dissolve salt in water, then evaporate the water. Ask: 'If a new substance was formed, how did we get the salt back unchanged?' The recovery demonstrates that dissolving is physical, not chemical.

teacher_glossary.definition: A mixture in which solid particles are dispersed in a liquid but are large enough to settle over time and to be removed by filtering. Suspensions are visibly cloudy because the particles are large enough to scatter light. Muddy water is a common example — the sediment settles if left undisturbed.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse suspensions with solutions — if both are 'stuff in liquid,' the distinction between dissolved (molecular-level) and suspended (visible particles) is missed.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The solution/suspension distinction determines which separation technique works — filtering separates suspensions but not solutions. If students confuse them, they cannot select appropriate separation methods.
teacher_glossary.response: Compare salt water (solution — clear, passes through filter) with muddy water (suspension — cloudy, trapped by filter). The filter test makes the particle-size distinction observable.

teacher_glossary.definition: A mixture in which particles are larger than in a solution but smaller than in a suspension — they remain dispersed and do not settle. Colloids often appear cloudy or opaque and cannot be separated by simple filtering. Milk, fog and gelatin are common examples. Colloids sit between solutions and suspensions in particle size.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students cannot distinguish colloids from solutions or suspensions — the intermediate particle size makes classification difficult.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Colloids demonstrate that mixture classification is a continuum based on particle size, not a simple binary. Understanding the continuum helps students select appropriate separation techniques and recognise why some methods fail for colloids.
teacher_glossary.response: Present solution, colloid and suspension side by side (salt water, milk, muddy water). Test each with a filter and a light beam (Tyndall effect). The comparative approach makes the particle-size continuum visible.

teacher_glossary.definition: A diagram showing the arrangement of atoms or molecules in a substance using circles to represent atoms, with different colours or sizes for different atom types. Particle diagrams show whether atoms are bonded (compound — atoms connected) or unbonded (mixture — atoms of different types present but not connected). They make the compound/mixture distinction visible at the model level.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students draw particle diagrams without distinguishing bonded from unbonded particles — elements, compounds and mixtures all look the same in their diagrams.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If particle diagrams do not show the bonded/unbonded distinction, the visual representation fails to convey the key difference between compounds and mixtures. The diagram should make classification visible — bonded = compound; unbonded = mixture.
teacher_glossary.response: Draw diagrams of the same atoms in two arrangements: bonded in fixed ratios (compound) and unbonded in variable proportions (mixture). Ask students to identify which is which and explain what the diagram shows.

teacher_glossary.definition: A 2D representation of a molecule showing which atoms are bonded to which, using lines to represent bonds. Structural formulas show bonding connections and arrangement that molecular formulas do not — H₂O could be H-O-H or H-H-O; the structural formula shows it is H-O-H. They are intermediate between compact molecular formulas and full 3D models.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse structural formulas with particle diagrams — miss that structural formulas show specific bonding connections between atoms, not just relative positions.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If structural formulas and particle diagrams are the same, students cannot read bonding information from the representation. The line = bond convention is the new information structural formulas provide beyond particle diagrams.
teacher_glossary.response: Present the same molecule as a molecular formula (H₂O), a particle diagram and a structural formula (H-O-H). Ask what new information each representation adds. The structural formula adds bonding connections that the others do not show.

teacher_glossary.definition: A 3D physical or digital representation of a molecule showing spatial arrangement, bond angles and relative atom sizes. Molecular models reveal information that 2D representations cannot — bond angles, molecular shape and relative atom sizes. At Year 8, ball-and-stick and space-filling are the two main model types.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think 3D models are just 'pretty versions' of 2D formulas — miss that 3D models convey spatial information (bond angles, molecular shape) that flat representations cannot.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If 3D models add nothing beyond aesthetics, students cannot explain why different representations exist or select the most appropriate one for a given purpose. Each representation type exists because it conveys different information.
teacher_glossary.response: Show water as a formula (H₂O), a structural formula (H-O-H) and a 3D model (bent shape, 104.5° angle). Ask what the 3D model shows that the others cannot. The bent shape is invisible in 2D — that is why 3D models exist.

sub_terms.definition: A 3D model using spheres for atoms and sticks for bonds. Shows bond connections and angles clearly but does not represent relative atom sizes accurately.
A 3D model using spheres sized proportionally to actual atoms, showing how much space each atom occupies. Shows molecular shape and size realistically but bonds are not visible.

teacher_glossary.definition: A change in which particles rearrange without forming new substances — atom types and bonding remain unchanged. Physical changes include melting, freezing, dissolving, tearing and bending. They are typically reversible because no new substance has formed, but reversibility is a consequence, not the definition — some physical changes (tearing paper) are difficult to reverse in practice.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students define physical change by reversibility rather than by the absence of new substance formation — this produces systematic misclassification of dissolving (reversible, sometimes classified as chemical) and some reactions.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The reversibility heuristic from AC9S6U04 works for most cases but fails for dissolving and for some chemical reactions that can be reversed. The new substance criterion must replace reversibility as the primary classification tool — otherwise students carry an unreliable test into Year 9 chemistry.
teacher_glossary.response: Present dissolving as the key test case: it is reversible (evaporate the water, get the salt back) but is it chemical? No — no new substance was formed. The test case makes the criterion replace reversibility.

teacher_glossary.definition: The ability of a change to be undone, returning the substance to its original state. At Year 8, reversibility is explicitly reframed — it is a consequence of physical change (no new substance means the original can be recovered) rather than its definition. The reversibility heuristic from AC9S6U04 is replaced by the new substance criterion because reversibility fails as a classifier in ambiguous cases.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students retain reversibility as the primary test for distinguishing physical from chemical change — 'if you can undo it, it is physical; if you cannot, it is chemical.'
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The reversibility test fails for dissolving (reversible, but not chemical? — correct) and for some chemical reactions that can be reversed under specific conditions. Students who retain this heuristic will misclassify changes throughout secondary chemistry.
teacher_glossary.response: Present two counterexamples: dissolving (reversible, physical) and thermal decomposition of limestone (chemical, but reversible under the right conditions). Both break the reversibility heuristic. Ask: 'If reversibility does not reliably distinguish the two, what does?' The answer is new substance formation.

teacher_glossary.definition: The process by which a solute disperses into a solvent at the molecular level, forming a solution. At the particle level, ionic or molecular units separate and distribute among solvent particles — no new compound is formed, which is why dissolving is a physical change despite the solid appearing to 'disappear.' Dissolving is the most commonly misclassified change — it looks chemical (solid vanishes) but the solute can be recovered by evaporation, confirming no new substance was formed.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students classify dissolving as a chemical change because the solid 'disappears' — the visual evidence of disappearance overrides the new substance criterion.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Dissolving is the diagnostic case for the physical/chemical distinction. Students who misclassify it have not internalised the new substance criterion and are likely still using the appearance-based or reversibility heuristic.
teacher_glossary.response: Dissolve salt in water, then evaporate. Ask: 'If dissolving were chemical, a new substance would have formed — could you get the salt back unchanged?' Recovery of the original substance is proof of physical change.

teacher_glossary.definition: A change in which bonds between atoms break and new bonds form, producing one or more new substances with different properties from the starting materials. Chemical change is defined by new substance formation — not by reversibility, colour change, or any single indicator. The new substance has a different chemical formula and different properties from the reactants.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students classify changes as chemical based on dramatic appearance changes (colour, bubbles, smell) rather than applying the new substance criterion — they confuse indicators with the definition.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If appearance changes define chemical change, students will classify some physical changes (dissolving a coloured solid) as chemical and miss some chemical changes (rusting, which is slow and visually subtle). The new substance criterion is the reliable test; indicators are evidence, not proof.
teacher_glossary.response: Present a change with dramatic appearance (dissolving coloured drink mix — physical) and one with subtle appearance (rusting — chemical). The mismatch between drama and classification forces the new substance criterion as the reliable test.

sub_terms.definition: The particle-level mechanism of chemical change — bonds in reactants break, and atoms rearrange and form new bonds to produce products with new properties.
The slow chemical reaction between iron, oxygen and water that produces iron oxide — a common everyday example of chemical change that is difficult to reverse.

teacher_glossary.definition: The principle that chemical change is defined by the formation of a new substance — a substance with a different chemical formula and different properties from the starting materials. The new substance criterion replaces the reversibility heuristic from AC9S6U04 as the primary classification tool. It is grounded in AC9S8U06's compound concept — a new compound is a new substance.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students state the criterion but do not apply it — they revert to reversibility or appearance when classifying actual changes.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The criterion is only useful if it is applied. Students who can state it but default to other tests will misclassify dissolving, slow reactions and ambiguous cases. Fluency requires practice applying the criterion to novel examples.
teacher_glossary.response: Present five unfamiliar changes and require students to classify each using only the new substance criterion — not reversibility, not appearance. The practice builds application fluency beyond stated knowledge.

teacher_glossary.definition: A substance that enters a chemical reaction — the starting material that is consumed and transformed into products. In the reaction between iron and oxygen to form rust, iron and oxygen are the reactants. Reactants appear on the left side of a chemical equation. Identifying reactants and products is the first step in describing any chemical change.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse reactants with products, or do not recognise that reactants are consumed during the reaction.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If reactants and products are confused, students cannot describe chemical changes correctly, cannot write word equations, and cannot apply conservation of mass in Year 9. The before/after distinction is foundational.
teacher_glossary.response: Use 'before and after' framing consistently: 'What substances were present before the reaction? Those are reactants. What substances are present after? Those are products.' The temporal framing is more intuitive than left/right in an equation.

teacher_glossary.definition: A substance produced by a chemical reaction — the new material formed when reactants are transformed. Products have different properties from reactants because they are different substances with different chemical formulas. In combustion of methane, carbon dioxide and water are the products. Products appear on the right side of a chemical equation.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think products are always solids or visible substances — miss that gaseous products (CO₂, water vapour) are equally valid and often escape unnoticed.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If gaseous products are missed, students cannot account for mass changes in reactions (mass appears to decrease when gas escapes) and cannot apply conservation of mass in Year 9.
teacher_glossary.response: Burn a candle and ask: 'Where did the wax go?' It became CO₂ and water vapour — gaseous products that escaped into the air. The 'missing' mass is in the gas.

teacher_glossary.definition: A process in which reactants are transformed into products through bond breaking and bond forming. Chemical reactions involve the rearrangement of atoms — atoms from the reactants are recombined into new arrangements in the products. At Year 8, reactions are described using word equations and observable indicators. Chemical equations with symbols are developed at Year 9.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think atoms are created or destroyed during reactions — miss that the same atoms are present before and after, just rearranged.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If atoms are created or destroyed, conservation of mass fails. The atoms-rearrange-but-are-not-created-or-destroyed principle is the foundation of conservation of mass in AC9S9U07 and equation balancing.
teacher_glossary.response: Use physical models (coloured balls for atoms) to build reactant molecules, then break them apart and rebuild as products. Count the atoms before and after — the same atoms in different arrangements. Nothing was created or destroyed.

teacher_glossary.definition: An observable sign that suggests a chemical change may have occurred. The four main indicators at Year 8 are gas production, precipitate formation, colour change and temperature change. Critically, indicators are evidence that suggests new substance formation — they are not the definition of chemical change. Some indicators can occur during physical changes (temperature change during dissolving), so indicators must be interpreted alongside the new substance criterion.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students invert the indicator-criterion relationship — they define chemical change by the presence of indicators rather than using indicators as evidence for the new substance criterion.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If indicators define chemical change, any colour change or temperature change is classified as chemical — including many physical changes. The evidence-criterion hierarchy (indicators suggest → criterion confirms) is essential for reliable classification.
teacher_glossary.response: Present a physical change with an indicator (dissolving coloured drink mix — colour change, temperature change) and a chemical change without dramatic indicators (slow rusting). Ask: 'Do indicators always mean chemical change? Does chemical change always show indicators?' Both answers are no — indicators are evidence, not proof.

sub_terms.definition: The appearance of bubbles or a new odour during a change, suggesting a gaseous compound has formed.
A change in the colour of a substance during a reaction, suggesting a new compound with different light-absorbing properties has formed.
A rise or fall in temperature during a change, suggesting energy is being released or absorbed as bonds break and form. Also occurs in some physical changes.

teacher_glossary.definition: An insoluble solid that forms when two solutions are mixed and a chemical reaction produces a compound that cannot dissolve. The precipitate appears as cloudiness or a visible solid settling out of the solution. Precipitate formation is one of the strongest indicators of chemical change because an insoluble new substance has clearly been produced.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse precipitates with sediment or undissolved material — miss that a precipitate is a new substance produced by a reaction, not something that was already present.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If precipitates are just settling solids, students cannot distinguish chemical precipitation (new substance formed) from physical settling (existing substance settling). The distinction is important for solution chemistry in Year 9.
teacher_glossary.response: Mix two clear solutions that produce a precipitate (e.g. lead nitrate + potassium iodide → yellow lead iodide precipitate). Ask: 'Both solutions were clear. Where did the solid come from?' The answer — a new substance was produced by the reaction — makes precipitate formation mechanistic.

teacher_glossary.definition: A chemical reaction that releases energy to the surroundings, observed as a temperature rise. In exothermic reactions, the energy released when product bonds form exceeds the energy required to break reactant bonds — the excess is released as heat. Combustion, neutralisation and cellular respiration are exothermic. Connects to AC9S8U05's energy transformation: chemical potential energy → thermal energy.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think exothermic means 'hot reaction' without understanding the bond energy mechanism — they identify exothermic by temperature rise but cannot explain why energy is released.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If exothermic is just 'gets hot,' students cannot explain the energy source or predict whether a reaction will be exothermic. The bond energy mechanism (products release more than reactants absorb) is the reasoning tool for Year 9 energy profile diagrams.
teacher_glossary.response: Ask: 'Where does the heat come from in combustion? Is it from the flame? From the fuel?' The answer — from the difference between energy needed to break reactant bonds and energy released when product bonds form — makes the mechanism explicit.

sub_terms.definition: A chemical reaction between an acid and a base that produces a salt and water, releasing thermal energy as an exothermic process.

The environment around a reaction system — the air, container and any substances not directly involved in the reaction. In exothermic reactions, energy transfers to the surroundings; in endothermic reactions, energy transfers from the surroundings.

teacher_glossary.definition: A chemical reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings, observed as a temperature drop. In endothermic reactions, the energy required to break reactant bonds exceeds the energy released when product bonds form — the deficit is absorbed from the surroundings as heat. Photosynthesis and thermal decomposition are endothermic. Cold packs exploit endothermic dissolving.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think endothermic means 'cold reaction' or 'no energy involved' — miss that endothermic reactions require energy input, absorbed from the surroundings.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If endothermic means 'no energy,' students cannot explain why the surroundings cool or why photosynthesis requires light energy input. The complement with exothermic — energy released vs energy absorbed — is the conceptual framework for reaction energetics.
teacher_glossary.response: Dissolve ammonium nitrate in water and measure the temperature drop. Ask: 'The solution got colder — where did the energy go?' The answer — into breaking bonds — makes the absorption mechanism tangible. Compare directly with an exothermic example.

sub_terms.definition: A chemical reaction in which a compound is broken down into simpler substances by heating — an endothermic process requiring continuous energy input.
The process by which plants use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen — an endothermic reaction that stores energy in chemical bonds.

teacher_glossary.definition: The amount of energy stored in a chemical bond — equivalently, the amount of energy required to break that bond. In chemical reactions, energy is required to break reactant bonds (energy input) and energy is released when product bonds form (energy output). The difference between these determines whether a reaction is exothermic (output > input) or endothermic (input > output). Bond energy reasoning is the mechanism underlying all reaction energetics.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think breaking bonds releases energy — the opposite is true. Breaking bonds requires energy input; forming bonds releases energy.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If breaking bonds releases energy, the exothermic/endothermic mechanism is inverted. This is one of the most persistent misconceptions in secondary chemistry and directly interferes with energy profile diagram interpretation in Year 9.
teacher_glossary.response: Use the magnet analogy: pulling two magnets apart requires effort (energy input = breaking bonds). Letting them snap together releases energy (energy output = forming bonds). Ask: 'Does separating require energy or release it?' The physical experience corrects the misconception.

student_glossary.definition: The smallest living building block of all organisms. Some living things are made of one cell; your body is made of trillions of cells, each too small to see without a microscope.
student_glossary.example: Your body contains many types of cells including skin cells, blood cells and muscle cells — each with a different job.

sub_terms.definition: A cell with a cell wall, chloroplasts (in green parts) and a large central vacuole — structural features that distinguish it from animal cells.
A cell without a cell wall, chloroplasts or large central vacuole — typically smaller and rounder than plant cells.
Too small to see with the unaided eye — requiring a microscope to observe. Most cells are microscopic.

student_glossary.definition: Making something appear larger so you can see more detail. Magnification changes the image, not the real object.
student_glossary.example: A microscope magnifies cells so their shapes and parts become visible, but the cells themselves stay the same tiny size.

student_glossary.definition: A photo taken through a microscope showing what real cells look like at high magnification.
student_glossary.example: A photomicrograph of a leaf cell shows green chloroplasts that you can't see with your eyes alone.

student_glossary.definition: The idea that all living things are made of cells — animals, plants, fungi and even tiny single-celled organisms.
student_glossary.example: A tree is living, so it is made of cells — even though tree cells look very different from your cells.

student_glossary.definition: A living thing made of just one cell. That one cell does everything the organism needs to survive — eating, growing and reproducing.
student_glossary.example: Bacteria are single-celled organisms — each bacterium is one complete living thing.

student_glossary.definition: A living thing made of many cells. Different cells often have different jobs.
student_glossary.example: Humans are multicellular — your body has over 200 different types of cells working together.

student_glossary.definition: Organisms that are made of cells. At Year 8, being made of cells is the key test for whether something is alive — not whether it moves or looks alive.
student_glossary.example: A mushroom doesn't move, but it's alive because it's made of cells. A robot moves, but it's not alive because it has no cells.

student_glossary.definition: A structure inside the cell that acts as the control centre. It contains DNA — the instructions that tell the cell what to do.
student_glossary.example: Without a nucleus, a cell wouldn't know which proteins to make or how to grow and divide.

student_glossary.definition: A thin boundary around every cell that controls what goes in and out. It lets useful substances in and keeps harmful ones out.
student_glossary.example: The cell membrane is like a security gate — it checks what's trying to enter and decides whether to let it through.

student_glossary.definition: The jelly-like material filling the inside of a cell. It's where many of the cell's chemical reactions happen, and it holds the organelles in place.
student_glossary.example: In a cell model, the cytoplasm would be the jelly holding all the parts — it's not empty space.

student_glossary.definition: Describes something that lets some things through but blocks others. The cell membrane is selectively permeable — it chooses what enters and leaves the cell.
student_glossary.example: A tea bag is selectively permeable — it lets water and flavour through but keeps the tea leaves inside.

student_glossary.definition: A molecule inside the nucleus that carries the instructions for everything the cell does — like a recipe book for building proteins.
student_glossary.example: Every cell in your body has the same DNA, but different cells read different parts of it — that's why a muscle cell is different from a skin cell.

student_glossary.definition: A strong outer layer found in plant cells that provides support and shape. It sits outside the cell membrane and keeps the cell rigid — like a frame around a balloon.
student_glossary.example: Plant stems stay upright partly because each cell has a rigid wall holding its shape.

student_glossary.definition: A structure in plant cells that uses light to make food for the plant through photosynthesis. Chloroplasts contain green pigment, which is why many plant parts are green.
student_glossary.example: Leaf cells have many chloroplasts because leaves are where plants catch the most light.

sub_terms.definition: The green pigment inside chloroplasts that captures light energy for photosynthesis.

student_glossary.definition: A large storage space in plant cells filled with fluid. It stores water and helps keep the cell firm — like an inflated balloon pressing against the cell wall.
student_glossary.example: When a plant wilts, its cells have lost water from their vacuoles and gone floppy.

student_glossary.definition: The process plants use to make their own food. Chloroplasts capture light energy and use it to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose (sugar) and oxygen.
student_glossary.example: Plants don't eat food like animals do — they make glucose in their leaves using sunlight.

student_glossary.definition: A living thing that makes its own food rather than eating other organisms. Plants are autotrophs because they produce glucose through photosynthesis.
student_glossary.example: Plants are autotrophs — they don't need to eat anything because they make food from sunlight, water and CO₂.

sub_terms.definition: An organism that obtains energy by consuming other organisms rather than producing its own food — animals, fungi and most bacteria.

student_glossary.definition: The pressure created by water inside a plant cell's vacuole pushing outward against the cell wall. This pressure keeps plant cells firm and plants upright.
student_glossary.example: A well-watered plant stands tall because its cells are full of water creating turgor pressure — a dehydrated plant wilts because the pressure drops.

student_glossary.definition: The tissue inside a leaf where photosynthesis happens. Mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts, unlike root cells which have none because they're underground.
student_glossary.example: If you slice a leaf in half and look through a microscope, the green mesophyll cells in the middle are doing the photosynthesis.

student_glossary.definition: A small structure inside a cell that has a specific job. Different organelles do different things — the nucleus controls, mitochondria release energy, ribosomes make proteins.
student_glossary.example: Organelles are to a cell what organs are to your body — each one has its own important function.

student_glossary.definition: Organelles that release usable energy from food. They don't create energy — they convert the energy stored in glucose into a form the cell can use. Cells that need lots of energy have many mitochondria.
student_glossary.example: Muscle cells contain many mitochondria because muscles use a lot of energy when you move.

student_glossary.definition: Tiny organelles that build proteins. Even though they're small, they're essential — proteins are needed for almost everything a cell does.
student_glossary.example: A cell that makes lots of protein, like one that produces digestive enzymes, needs many ribosomes.

student_glossary.definition: The way different cells develop different features to do different jobs. A muscle cell looks and works differently from a nerve cell because each is specialised for its function.
student_glossary.example: Red blood cells are disc-shaped to carry oxygen efficiently — their shape is a specialisation for their job.

sub_terms.definition: The specific set of organelles present in a cell, varying between cell types to match their function.
A cell with structural features adapted for a particular function — such as red blood cells for oxygen transport or root hair cells for water absorption.

student_glossary.definition: A chemical process inside mitochondria that releases energy from food. It's not the same as breathing — breathing gets oxygen to your cells, but respiration is the chemical reaction inside cells that actually releases the energy.
student_glossary.example: Both plant and animal cells carry out cellular respiration — even plants need to release energy from food, not just make it.

student_glossary.definition: The process of building proteins from smaller building blocks, carried out by ribosomes using instructions from DNA. Proteins do many of the cell's most important jobs.
student_glossary.example: When your body heals a cut, cells near the wound ramp up protein synthesis to build new tissue.

student_glossary.definition: A condition where mitochondria don't work properly, so cells can't release enough energy. This especially affects parts of the body that need the most energy, like muscles and the brain.
student_glossary.example: Someone with mitochondrial disease might feel very tired and have weak muscles because their cells can't release enough energy from food.

student_glossary.definition: The reason tissues exist — because cells specialise for different jobs, cells with the same specialisation naturally group together to work as a team. Specialisation creates variety, and that variety is what builds tissues, organs and organ systems.
student_glossary.example: Muscle cells are all specialised for contraction, so they group together as muscle tissue. Nerve cells are specialised for signal transmission, so they group as nerve tissue. Specialisation is the starting point for the whole hierarchy.

student_glossary.definition: The particular set of organelles a cell has, including how many of each. Different specialised cells have different organelle complements to match their jobs.
student_glossary.example: Muscle cells have about 2000 mitochondria because contraction uses huge amounts of energy, while a skin cell might only have 300.

sub_terms.definition: An organelle that packages and sends out proteins and other molecules the cell has made.

student_glossary.definition: A specialised cell designed to carry oxygen through your blood. It has a squished disc shape for maximum surface area, no nucleus to make more room for haemoglobin, and is flexible enough to squeeze through tiny blood vessels.
student_glossary.example: Every feature of a red blood cell helps it carry oxygen — even losing its nucleus makes more room for the oxygen-carrying molecule haemoglobin.

sub_terms.definition: A shape that curves inward on both sides, like a squished ball — this gives the cell more surface area.
The iron-containing protein in red blood cells that binds to oxygen molecules for transport through the bloodstream.

student_glossary.definition: A specialised plant cell that carries water from roots up to leaves. Xylem cells are actually dead and hollow — like tiny drainpipes with thick, rigid walls.
student_glossary.example: A xylem cell works because it is hollow and dead — if it still had cytoplasm and organelles inside, water could not flow through it easily.

student_glossary.definition: A specialised cell that carries electrical signals around your body. Nerve cells can be extremely long — up to a metre — with branching ends to connect to other cells.
student_glossary.example: A nerve cell running from your spinal cord to your foot can be almost a metre long — its extreme length lets it carry signals over that whole distance.

sub_terms.definition: The long part of a nerve cell that carries signals away from the cell body.
Short branching parts of a nerve cell that pick up incoming signals from other cells.

student_glossary.definition: A specialised cell that contracts to produce movement. Muscle cells are elongated and packed with mitochondria because contraction uses a lot of energy.
student_glossary.example: Muscle cells have thousands of mitochondria — contraction is hard work, so the cell needs lots of energy-producing organelles.

student_glossary.definition: A group of similar specialised cells that work together to do one job. A tissue is not just any group of cells near each other — the cells must be the same type and share a function.
student_glossary.example: Muscle tissue is made of many muscle cells contracting together — one muscle cell alone could not move your arm, but thousands working as a tissue can.

student_glossary.definition: A tissue made of muscle cells that contracts to produce movement. Found not just in your arms and legs, but also in your heart, stomach and other internal organs.
student_glossary.example: Your heart is constantly contracting because it contains cardiac muscle tissue — a type of muscle tissue that never gets tired.

sub_terms.definition: The special muscle tissue in your heart that contracts rhythmically on its own without you thinking about it.

student_glossary.definition: A tissue made of tightly packed cells that covers surfaces and lines the inside of organs, providing protection. It is not just skin — it lines your blood vessels, stomach and lungs too.
student_glossary.example: The inside of your stomach is lined with epithelial tissue that protects the stomach wall from the acid inside.

sub_terms.definition: A tightly packed cell that forms epithelial tissue — flat, thin cells arranged in sheets to cover surfaces and line organs.

student_glossary.definition: A plant tissue made of many hollow xylem cells stacked end-to-end to form long tubes that carry water from roots to leaves.
student_glossary.example: A single hollow xylem cell is like one section of pipe — many of them joined together form the xylem tissue that can carry water to the top of a tall tree.

student_glossary.definition: A plant tissue that carries dissolved sugars from the leaves (where they are made by photosynthesis) to other parts of the plant that need energy.
student_glossary.example: When a fruit is growing, phloem tissue delivers sugar from the leaves to the fruit — that is why fruit tastes sweet.

sub_terms.definition: A living plant cell with perforated end walls that forms phloem tissue, allowing dissolved sugars to flow through.

student_glossary.definition: A body part made of several different types of tissue working together to do a job. No single tissue type can do everything an organ needs — that is why organs contain multiple tissues.
student_glossary.example: Your heart has muscle tissue (to pump), epithelial tissue (to line the inside smoothly) and connective tissue (to hold it together) — all three are needed for it to work.
