student_glossary.definition: A tissue that provides structural support and holds other tissues and organs together. Bone, cartilage and tendons are all types of connective tissue.
student_glossary.example: The framework that holds your heart in shape and connects it to blood vessels is connective tissue — without it, the heart would have no structure.

student_glossary.definition: A group of organs that work together to carry out a major job the body needs to survive. If one organ in the system fails, the whole system is affected.
student_glossary.example: Your circulatory system includes the heart, blood vessels and blood — if any one of these fails, oxygen cannot reach your cells.

student_glossary.definition: The organ system that moves blood around your body, delivering oxygen and nutrients to cells and carrying away waste. It includes the heart, blood vessels and blood.
student_glossary.example: When you exercise, your circulatory system works harder — your heart pumps faster to deliver more oxygen to your muscles through your blood vessels.

sub_terms.definition: The tubes (arteries, veins and capillaries) that carry blood between the heart and every part of your body.

student_glossary.definition: The organ system that breaks down food into nutrients your body can use. Each organ does a different stage — your mouth chews, your stomach uses acid, your intestines absorb nutrients.
student_glossary.example: Digestion does not just happen in the stomach — by the time food reaches your small intestine, it has already been broken down by your mouth and stomach first.

student_glossary.definition: A plant's transport system, made up of xylem (carrying water up) and phloem (carrying sugar around). It works like the circulatory system in animals but uses different structures.
student_glossary.example: A plant's vascular system solves the same problem as your circulatory system — getting essential substances to every part of the organism.

student_glossary.definition: The thin, solid outer layer of Earth that we live on. There are two types — oceanic crust under the oceans (thinner and denser) and continental crust forming the continents (thicker and lighter).
student_glossary.example: If Earth were an apple, the crust would be thinner than the apple's skin.

sub_terms.definition: The thinner, denser type of crust found under the oceans. Because it is denser, it gets pushed under continental crust when they collide.
The thicker, lighter type of crust that forms the continents. Because it is lighter, it does not sink — when two pieces collide, they crumple upward into mountains.

student_glossary.definition: The thick layer between Earth's crust and core. It is solid rock, but under extreme heat and pressure it flows very slowly — like a glacier flowing downhill, but even slower.
student_glossary.example: The mantle flows at about the same speed your fingernails grow — centimetres per year. This slow flow is what moves the tectonic plates above.

student_glossary.definition: The liquid layer of Earth between the mantle and the inner core, made mostly of iron and nickel. It is the only truly liquid layer inside Earth.
student_glossary.example: The outer core is liquid metal — its heat drives the slow flow in the mantle above, which in turn moves the plates at Earth's surface.

student_glossary.definition: The solid centre of Earth, made of iron and nickel. Even though it is the hottest part of Earth, the incredible pressure keeps it solid.
student_glossary.example: The inner core is hotter than the surface of the Sun, but the pressure at Earth's centre is so extreme that the metal cannot melt.

student_glossary.definition: The rigid outer shell of Earth, made of the crust plus the very top of the mantle. This is the layer that is broken into tectonic plates.
student_glossary.example: Tectonic plates are not just the crust — they include a layer of rigid mantle underneath, and the whole thing moves as one piece.

student_glossary.definition: The soft, slowly flowing layer of the upper mantle just below the lithosphere. The tectonic plates sit on top of it and are moved by its slow flow.
student_glossary.example: Think of the asthenosphere like warm toffee — it is technically solid, but it can flow very slowly when pushed. The plates ride on top of this flow.

sub_terms.definition: An ancient, stable section of continental crust that has remained largely unchanged for billions of years, forming the core of a continent.

student_glossary.definition: A large, rigid piece of Earth's lithosphere that moves as one unit. There are about 15 major plates, and they move a few centimetres each year — about the speed your fingernails grow.
student_glossary.example: Australia sits on the Indo-Australian Plate, which is slowly moving northward. Over millions of years, this movement will change where Australia is on the globe.

student_glossary.definition: The slow circular movement of hot rock in the mantle. Hot material rises toward the surface, cools, then sinks back down — this circulation creates forces that push and pull the tectonic plates.
student_glossary.example: Mantle convection works like heating soup — hot soup rises, cools at the surface and sinks again. The same cycle in the mantle moves the plates above.

sub_terms.definition: When a heavy plate sinks into the mantle at a subduction zone, it drags the rest of the plate with it — like a heavy blanket sliding off a bed.
When new crust at a mid-ocean ridge pushes outward and away, shoving the rest of the plate along.

student_glossary.definition: The zone where two tectonic plates meet. Most earthquakes and volcanoes happen at plate boundaries because this is where plates interact.
student_glossary.example: Japan sits right on a plate boundary, which is why it experiences frequent earthquakes and has many volcanoes.

student_glossary.definition: A place where two plates move apart. Magma rises up to fill the gap and creates new crust. This is how mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys form.
student_glossary.example: In the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, two plates are slowly pulling apart — magma rises to fill the gap, building the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

sub_terms.definition: A long, low area that forms where a continent is being pulled apart, before it fully splits. The East African Rift is forming this way right now.

student_glossary.definition: The ongoing process where new ocean floor is created at mid-ocean ridges as magma rises and hardens, pushing older crust outward on both sides.
student_glossary.example: The Atlantic Ocean is getting a few centimetres wider every year because new crust keeps forming at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and pushing outward.

student_glossary.definition: An underwater mountain chain where new ocean floor is being created. Mid-ocean ridges are the longest mountain ranges on Earth — they stretch over 65,000 km across all the world's oceans.
student_glossary.example: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs all the way from the Arctic to near Antarctica — it is longer than the Andes, Himalayas and Rockies combined.

student_glossary.definition: A place where two plates move toward each other and collide. What happens depends on which types of crust collide — if one is oceanic, it sinks under the other; if both are continental, they crumple upward into mountains.
student_glossary.example: The Himalayas are still growing because the Indian Plate is crashing into the Eurasian Plate — neither sinks, so the land folds and pushes upward.

sub_terms.definition: A very deep valley on the ocean floor where one plate is being pushed under another.
A curved line of volcanoes that forms alongside an ocean trench, where the sinking plate melts and magma rises to the surface.
A chain of mountains formed when two continents collide and the land crumples and pushes upward because neither plate can sink.
A horseshoe-shaped zone of intense volcanic and earthquake activity around the Pacific Ocean, marking convergent and transform plate boundaries.

student_glossary.definition: When a denser plate is pushed under a lighter plate and sinks down into the mantle. The sinking plate melts and gets recycled. This creates trenches, volcanoes and deep earthquakes.
student_glossary.example: Along the west coast of South America, the oceanic plate is being pushed under the continent and sinking into the mantle — this created the Andes mountains and the deep Peru-Chile Trench.

student_glossary.definition: A place where two plates slide sideways past each other. The friction between the plates causes stress to build up and release suddenly as earthquakes. No volcanoes form here because no magma is involved.
student_glossary.example: The San Andreas Fault in California is a transform boundary — it causes earthquakes but no volcanic eruptions, because the plates are sliding past each other, not pulling apart or colliding.

sub_terms.definition: A crack in the Earth where the rock on each side moves sideways rather than up and down.
A major transform plate boundary in California where the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other, producing frequent earthquakes.

student_glossary.definition: The observation that some continents look like they fit together like puzzle pieces — especially South America and Africa. This suggests they were once joined together.
student_glossary.example: If you cut out South America and Africa from a map and push them together, the coastlines match up remarkably well — as if they were once one piece of land.

student_glossary.definition: The finding that identical fossils of land animals and plants appear on continents that are now separated by oceans. Since these organisms could not have crossed oceans, the continents must have been joined when the organisms were alive.
student_glossary.example: Fossils of Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile, are found in both South America and Africa — it could not have swum across the Atlantic, so those continents must have been connected.

student_glossary.definition: The observation that ocean floor rock is youngest at mid-ocean ridges and gets older the further you go from the ridge, with matching ages on both sides. This is exactly what you would expect if new crust is constantly being made at the ridge.
student_glossary.example: Rock right at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is brand new. Rock near the coast of Africa is about 180 million years old. The age increases steadily — proof that the ocean floor has been spreading outward for millions of years.

student_glossary.definition: Rock formed from broken-down pieces of other rocks that have been squashed and cemented together over millions of years. You can often see layers in sedimentary rock and sometimes find fossils in it.
student_glossary.example: Sandstone is sedimentary rock — it formed from sand grains that were deposited in layers, buried and slowly cemented together.

student_glossary.definition: The breaking down of rock into smaller pieces, either by physical forces (like temperature changes cracking the rock) or chemical reactions (like acid rain dissolving minerals). Weathering happens where the rock sits — the pieces do not move yet.
student_glossary.example: When water seeps into a crack in a rock and freezes, it expands and breaks the rock apart — that is physical weathering.

sub_terms.definition: Breaking rock apart using physical forces like freezing water or growing tree roots, without changing what the rock is made of.
Breaking rock apart through chemical reactions, like acid rain slowly dissolving limestone.

student_glossary.definition: The movement of broken rock pieces by water, wind, ice or gravity to a new location. As pieces are carried, they bump into each other and become smaller and rounder.
student_glossary.example: River pebbles are smooth and round because they have been tumbled and worn down during erosion — the further they have travelled, the rounder they become.

sub_terms.definition: The movement of weathered rock fragments by water, wind, ice or gravity — the erosion step between weathering and deposition.

student_glossary.definition: When sediment that has been carried by water, wind or ice settles and builds up in a new place. Each time sediment settles, it forms a new layer on top of the previous one.
student_glossary.example: At the mouth of a river, the water slows down and drops the sediment it was carrying — layer after layer builds up over time.

student_glossary.definition: The process that turns loose sediment into solid rock. The weight of layers above squashes the sediment together (compaction), and minerals dissolved in water crystallise between the grains and glue them together (cementation).
student_glossary.example: Sand at the beach is loose — but if it were buried under hundreds of metres of more sand for millions of years, the pressure and mineral cement would turn it into sandstone.

sub_terms.definition: The squeezing of sediment layers under the weight of material above, pushing out water and air.
Natural minerals acting as glue between sediment grains, binding them into solid rock.

student_glossary.definition: Pieces of broken-down rock, ranging from tiny clay particles to large boulders. Sediment is the raw material that eventually becomes sedimentary rock.
student_glossary.example: Sand on a beach, mud at the bottom of a river and gravel in a creek bed are all sediment — broken pieces of rock that have been weathered and transported.

student_glossary.definition: The preserved remains or traces of a living thing, almost always found in sedimentary rock. Fossils form when organisms are buried by sediment before they fully break down.
student_glossary.example: A shell fossil in limestone tells you that the rock formed in an area that was once underwater, where the shell was buried by sediment millions of years ago.

student_glossary.definition: Rock formed when molten rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens. The size of the crystals tells you how fast it cooled — big crystals mean slow cooling underground, tiny crystals mean fast cooling at the surface.
student_glossary.example: Granite cooled slowly deep underground, which is why you can see large crystals in it. Basalt cooled quickly at the surface, so its crystals are too small to see easily.

student_glossary.definition: Molten rock that is still underground. When it cools underground, it forms igneous rock with large crystals because it cools slowly.
student_glossary.example: Granite formed from magma that cooled slowly deep inside Earth — the insulating rock around it kept it warm for a long time, giving big crystals time to grow.

student_glossary.definition: Molten rock that has reached Earth's surface, usually through a volcanic eruption. It is the same material as magma, but at the surface it cools much faster.
student_glossary.example: When lava flows from a volcano and hits the air, it cools rapidly — that is why basalt has tiny crystals you can barely see.

student_glossary.definition: Igneous rock that formed underground from slowly cooling magma. The slow cooling gives crystals plenty of time to grow large.
student_glossary.example: Granite is intrusive — it formed deep underground where the surrounding rock kept the magma warm, so large crystals had time to grow.

sub_terms.definition: A common intrusive igneous rock with large, visible crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica, formed from magma cooling slowly deep underground.

student_glossary.definition: Igneous rock that formed at Earth's surface from rapidly cooling lava. The fast cooling means crystals have little time to grow, so they are very small or the rock is glassy.
student_glossary.example: Obsidian cooled so fast that no crystals had time to form at all — it looks like shiny black glass.

sub_terms.definition: A common extrusive igneous rock with fine-grained crystals, formed from lava cooling rapidly at Earth's surface. The most common rock on the ocean floor.
A volcanic glass formed when lava cools so rapidly that no crystals have time to form, producing a smooth, glassy texture.

student_glossary.definition: How big the crystals are in an igneous rock. Crystal size tells you how fast the rock cooled — bigger crystals mean slower cooling, smaller crystals mean faster cooling.
student_glossary.example: If you find a rock with large visible crystals, you know it cooled slowly underground. If the crystals are tiny, it cooled quickly at the surface.

sub_terms.definition: How quickly molten rock loses heat and turns solid — slow underground, fast at the surface.
The process of crystals forming as molten rock cools and hardens.

student_glossary.definition: Rock that has been changed by extreme heat and pressure deep underground — but without melting. The minerals get squashed, realigned and recrystallised, making the rock harder and denser than the original.
student_glossary.example: Shale is a soft, layered sedimentary rock. Put it under extreme pressure and heat and it becomes slate — harder, denser and with minerals aligned in one direction.

sub_terms.definition: How much heat and pressure a rock experienced — more heat and pressure means bigger changes from the original.

student_glossary.definition: When the minerals in a rock reorganise into new crystal arrangements under heat and pressure, without the rock actually melting. This is what happens during metamorphism.
student_glossary.example: The calcite crystals in limestone get reorganised under heat and pressure into the interlocking crystals of marble — same mineral, new arrangement.

student_glossary.definition: The parallel stripes or layers you can see in metamorphic rock, caused by minerals being squashed and lined up in one direction by pressure. This looks similar to layers in sedimentary rock but forms in a completely different way.
student_glossary.example: The stripes in schist were created by intense pressure squashing the minerals flat and lining them up — unlike sedimentary layers, which formed from settling sediment.

student_glossary.definition: The original rock that a metamorphic rock formed from. The parent rock determines what the metamorphic rock will be, because the minerals are reorganised, not replaced.
student_glossary.example: Limestone is the parent rock of marble — the calcite minerals are the same, but heat and pressure reorganised them into a harder, more crystalline rock.

student_glossary.definition: The never-ending set of processes that transform rocks from one type to another over millions of years. Any rock type can become any other type — there is no fixed order. The rock cycle is driven by plate tectonics (providing heat, pressure and uplift) and surface processes (weathering and erosion).
student_glossary.example: A piece of granite (igneous) can be weathered into sand, deposited and turned into sandstone (sedimentary), then buried and squeezed into quartzite (metamorphic) — and if it melts, the cycle starts again.

student_glossary.definition: When tectonic forces push rock that formed deep underground up toward Earth's surface, where weathering and erosion can reach it. Without uplift, buried rocks would never return to the surface part of the rock cycle.
student_glossary.example: The granite in mountain ranges formed deep underground — tectonic forces pushed it up, and then millions of years of erosion wore away the rock above to expose it.

student_glossary.definition: The enormous time periods over which rock cycle processes happen — usually millions to hundreds of millions of years. Rocks seem permanent to us, but on Earth's timescale, no rock lasts forever.
student_glossary.example: If all of Earth's history were squeezed into one year, all of human civilisation would fit into the last few seconds of December 31st — rock cycle processes that seem impossibly slow are fast on this scale.

student_glossary.definition: A step-by-step identification tool that asks yes/no questions to narrow down what something is. For rocks, each question tests a property like crystal size or layering to work out the rock type.
student_glossary.example: A rock identification key might ask: 'Can you see layers?' If yes → could be sedimentary. 'Are there fossils?' If yes → sedimentary. Each question narrows it down.

student_glossary.definition: Energy that involves something actively happening — objects moving, particles vibrating, waves travelling or charges flowing. If something is in action, its energy is kinetic.
student_glossary.example: A moving car has kinetic energy, but so does a hot cup of tea — the water particles are vibrating rapidly, and that vibration IS the thermal (kinetic) energy.

sub_terms.definition: Energy carried by vibrating particles — when a speaker plays music, it vibrates the air, and that vibration travels to your ears.
Energy carried by light waves travelling through space.
Energy from electric charges flowing through a wire or circuit.
The energy of a moving object — a rolling ball, a swinging bat, a spinning wheel.

student_glossary.definition: The energy of particles vibrating inside a substance. The faster the particles move, the hotter the substance feels. Thermal energy is kinetic because the particles are actively moving — it is not stored energy.
student_glossary.example: A hot drink feels warm because its water particles are vibrating fast. As it cools, those particles slow down — the thermal energy transfers to the cooler surroundings.

student_glossary.definition: Stored energy that is not doing anything yet, but could be released. It depends on position (height), composition (chemical bonds) or shape (stretched/compressed).
student_glossary.example: A ball at the top of a ramp has gravitational potential energy — nothing is happening yet, but when it rolls, that stored energy converts to kinetic energy.

sub_terms.definition: Energy stored in the bonds of molecules — food, fuel and batteries all store chemical potential energy that is released in reactions.
Energy stored because of height — the higher up something is, the more energy it has stored.
Energy stored in something that has been stretched or squashed — a rubber band, a spring, a compressed ball.

student_glossary.definition: When energy moves from one place to another but stays the same type. The energy type does not change — only its location does.
student_glossary.example: When you hold a hot mug, heat moves from the mug to your hand — it is thermal energy before and thermal energy after, just in a different place.

student_glossary.definition: When energy changes from one type to a different type. Almost every transformation produces some by-product heat alongside the useful output.
student_glossary.example: A light bulb transforms electrical energy into light energy (useful) and heat energy (by-product) — that is why light bulbs get hot.

sub_terms.definition: A chemical reaction in which a fuel reacts with oxygen, releasing thermal and light energy. A common example of chemical potential energy transforming to kinetic energy.

student_glossary.definition: Unwanted thermal energy produced during almost every energy transformation. The energy is not lost or destroyed — it just ends up as heat that spreads into the surroundings instead of doing something useful.
student_glossary.example: Your phone gets warm when you use it because some of the electrical energy is transformed into heat instead of screen light or sound — that warmth is by-product heat.

sub_terms.definition: The type of energy a device is designed to produce — light from a lamp, movement from a motor.

student_glossary.definition: The rule that energy can never be created or destroyed — it can only change type or move to a different place. When energy seems to disappear, it has actually become by-product heat spreading into the surroundings.
student_glossary.example: When a ball bouncing on the floor gradually bounces lower, the energy is not disappearing — each bounce converts some kinetic energy into heat and sound, which spread into the surroundings.

student_glossary.definition: Following energy step by step through a system, naming the energy type at each stage and identifying all the transfers, transformations and by-products along the way.
student_glossary.example: Tracing a torch: chemical energy (battery) → electrical energy (circuit) → light energy (useful output) + heat energy (by-product). Every stage is accounted for.

student_glossary.definition: A diagram that shows energy moving through a system using arrows and labels. Every transformation stage needs arrows for both the useful output AND the by-product — if arrows are missing, the diagram does not add up.
student_glossary.example: A flow diagram for a car engine shows: chemical energy → kinetic energy (useful) + heat energy (by-product) + sound energy (by-product). All the arrows leaving a stage must add up to the energy entering it.

student_glossary.definition: The tiny particles that make up all matter. In Year 7, you learned about particles — now we know those particles are atoms, and different types of atoms make different elements.
student_glossary.example: Every piece of gold is made of gold atoms. Every breath of oxygen is made of oxygen atoms. The type of atom determines what the substance is.

student_glossary.definition: What kind of atom something is — each element has its own unique atom type. All atoms of the same element are identical; atoms of different elements are different types.
student_glossary.example: Carbon atoms and oxygen atoms are different atom types — that is why carbon (in pencil lead) and oxygen (in air) are completely different substances.

student_glossary.definition: The model you learned in Year 7 that describes matter as made of tiny particles with arrangement, motion and forces between them. In Year 8, we add one thing: those particles are atoms, and atoms have type.
student_glossary.example: You already know that particles in a solid are packed tightly and vibrate in place. Now add: those particles are atoms, and if they are all the same type, the solid is an element.

student_glossary.definition: A pure substance made of only one type of atom. Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances by any chemical process.
student_glossary.example: Copper wire is made of only copper atoms — it is an element. Aluminium foil is made of only aluminium atoms — it is also an element.

student_glossary.definition: A short abbreviation (one or two letters) for an element. The first letter is always a capital; the second is always lowercase. You can look up any element's symbol on the periodic table.
student_glossary.example: O = oxygen, Fe = iron, Na = sodium. Be careful: Co means cobalt (one element), but CO means carbon monoxide (a compound of carbon and oxygen).

student_glossary.definition: A chart that organises all known elements in order. Elements in the same column have similar properties. You use it like a reference tool — look up symbols, names and properties rather than trying to memorise it.
student_glossary.example: Need to know the symbol for gold? Find it on the periodic table — it is Au, from the Latin word 'aurum.'

student_glossary.definition: A substance made of two or more different types of atoms chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Compounds have completely different properties from the elements they are made of.
student_glossary.example: Table salt (NaCl) is a compound — but sodium on its own reacts violently with water, and chlorine is a toxic gas. Combined, they make something safe to eat. That is how different a compound is from its elements.

sub_terms.definition: The small number after an element symbol in a formula — it tells you how many atoms of that element. H₂O has a subscript 2 after H, meaning two hydrogen atoms.
Compounds always have the same proportion of atoms — water is always two hydrogen to one oxygen, never anything else.

student_glossary.definition: A shorthand way of writing what atoms are in a compound and how many of each. You use element symbols and small numbers (subscripts) to show the ratio.
student_glossary.example: CO₂ means one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms bonded together — that is carbon dioxide.

student_glossary.definition: The strong force of attraction holding atoms together in a compound. Bonds are not physical links like rope — they are forces, like the invisible pull between magnets.
student_glossary.example: In a water molecule, the oxygen atom is bonded to two hydrogen atoms. Breaking those bonds takes energy — that is why you need electricity to split water back into hydrogen and oxygen.

student_glossary.definition: A combination of substances that are mixed together but not chemically bonded. The components keep their own properties and can be separated using physical methods like filtering or evaporating.
student_glossary.example: Salt water is a mixture — the salt and water are mixed but not bonded. Evaporate the water and the salt is still there, unchanged.

sub_terms.definition: Mixtures can have different amounts of each component — you can make salt water saltier or less salty, unlike a compound which always has the same ratio.
Ways of getting mixture components apart using physical properties — filtering, evaporating, distilling.

student_glossary.definition: A mixture where one substance is completely dissolved in another, making a clear, even mixture. The dissolved substance is spread out so evenly that you cannot see it or filter it out.
student_glossary.example: Salt water looks clear because the salt particles are so tiny and spread out that light passes straight through — but the salt is still there.

student_glossary.definition: A cloudy mixture where solid particles are floating in a liquid but will eventually settle to the bottom. You can separate them by filtering.
student_glossary.example: Muddy water is a suspension — leave it long enough and the dirt settles to the bottom. You can also pour it through a filter and the water comes through clear.

student_glossary.definition: A mixture with particles bigger than in a solution but smaller than in a suspension — they stay spread out and do not settle. Colloids are often cloudy or opaque.
student_glossary.example: Milk is a colloid — the tiny fat droplets are spread through the water and do not settle, but they make the liquid look white instead of clear.

student_glossary.definition: A drawing showing how atoms are arranged in a substance, using different colours for different atom types. If atoms are connected, it is a compound; if they are just near each other, it is a mixture.
student_glossary.example: In a particle diagram of salt water, you would see NaCl units scattered among water molecules — the Na and Cl are separated but not bonded to the water.

student_glossary.definition: A flat drawing of a molecule that shows which atoms are bonded to which, using lines for bonds. It tells you more than a chemical formula because you can see the arrangement.
student_glossary.example: The chemical formula H₂O tells you there are 2 H and 1 O. The structural formula H-O-H tells you both hydrogens are bonded to the oxygen, not to each other.

student_glossary.definition: A 3D model of a molecule showing the actual shape, bond angles and relative sizes of atoms. It reveals things that flat drawings cannot — like the bent shape of a water molecule.
student_glossary.example: A ball-and-stick model of water shows that the molecule is bent, not straight — the two hydrogen atoms sit at an angle from the oxygen. You cannot see this in a flat formula.

sub_terms.definition: A 3D model using balls for atoms and sticks for bonds — good for seeing bond angles.
A 3D model where atoms are shown at their real relative sizes — good for seeing how much space a molecule takes up.

student_glossary.definition: A change where particles rearrange but no new substance is formed. The atoms stay bonded the same way — they just move to different positions. Physical changes can usually be reversed.
student_glossary.example: Melting ice is a physical change — the water molecules are the same before and after, they just move more freely as a liquid.

student_glossary.definition: Whether a change can be undone. Most physical changes are reversible and most chemical changes are not, but this is not a reliable test — some physical changes are hard to reverse and some chemical changes can be reversed.
student_glossary.example: Tearing paper is a physical change that is hard to reverse. Some chemical reactions can be reversed under special conditions. That is why 'can you undo it?' is not the best test.

student_glossary.definition: When a substance spreads out into a liquid at the particle level and seems to disappear. Dissolving is a physical change — no new substance is formed, even though the solid seems to vanish. You can prove this by evaporating the liquid and getting the solid back.
student_glossary.example: When you stir sugar into water, it disappears — but evaporate the water and the sugar is still there. No new substance was created, so dissolving is physical.

student_glossary.definition: A change where bonds between atoms break and new bonds form, creating one or more new substances. The new substances have different properties from what you started with.
student_glossary.example: When iron rusts, the iron atoms bond with oxygen atoms to form iron oxide — a completely different substance that is orange, flaky and crumbly instead of strong and shiny.

sub_terms.definition: The process inside a chemical change — old connections between atoms break apart, and the atoms rearrange into new connections.
The slow chemical reaction between iron, oxygen and water that produces iron oxide — a common everyday example of chemical change that is difficult to reverse.

student_glossary.definition: The rule that a change is chemical if and only if a new substance is formed — something with different properties and a different chemical formula from what you started with. This is a more reliable test than 'can you reverse it?'
student_glossary.example: Dissolving salt looks dramatic (the solid vanishes!) but no new substance forms — evaporate and the salt returns. Rusting looks subtle, but iron oxide is a completely different substance from iron. The new substance test gets it right both times.

student_glossary.definition: A substance you start with before a chemical reaction — it gets used up and transformed into something new.
student_glossary.example: When you burn wood, the wood and oxygen are the reactants — they are consumed during burning and transformed into ash, carbon dioxide and water.

student_glossary.definition: A new substance that is produced by a chemical reaction. Products have different properties from the reactants because they are different substances.
student_glossary.example: When you burn a candle, the products are carbon dioxide and water vapour — both are invisible gases, which is why the candle wax seems to 'disappear.'

student_glossary.definition: A process where reactants are transformed into products by breaking and forming bonds between atoms. The same atoms are present before and after — they are just rearranged into new combinations.
student_glossary.example: In the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to make water, no atoms are created or destroyed — the hydrogen and oxygen atoms are just rearranged into a new combination (H₂O).

student_glossary.definition: An observable clue that a chemical change might have happened — like bubbles, a colour change, a new smell or a temperature change. But indicators are clues, not proof — you still need to check whether a new substance was actually formed.
student_glossary.example: Dissolving coloured drink mix produces a colour change and temperature change — but it is physical, not chemical. Indicators suggest, they do not prove.

sub_terms.definition: Bubbles or a new smell appearing during a change — suggests a new gas is being produced.
The substance changing colour during a change — suggests a new substance with different light-absorbing properties.
The mixture getting hotter or colder — suggests energy is being released or absorbed as bonds break and form.

student_glossary.definition: A solid that forms when you mix two liquids together and a chemical reaction produces a new substance that cannot dissolve. The solid appears 'out of nowhere' because it was not there before — it was created by the reaction.
student_glossary.example: Mix two clear solutions and a bright yellow solid suddenly appears — that solid is a precipitate, a brand-new substance created by the reaction between the two solutions.

student_glossary.definition: A chemical reaction that releases energy, making the surroundings warmer. The energy comes from the bonds forming in the products — when products form, they release more energy than it took to break the reactant bonds.
student_glossary.example: Burning fuel is exothermic — the heat you feel is energy released when the product bonds (in CO₂ and H₂O) form.

sub_terms.definition: A chemical reaction between an acid and a base that produces a salt and water, releasing thermal energy as an exothermic process.
Everything around the reaction — the air, the container, your hand holding the test tube. In exothermic reactions, the surroundings get warmer.

student_glossary.definition: A chemical reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings, making them cooler. The reaction needs more energy to break reactant bonds than the product bonds release, so it takes heat from the surroundings.
student_glossary.example: A cold pack gets cold because the reaction inside absorbs heat from your skin — the surroundings (your hand) lose energy, which is why it feels cold.

sub_terms.definition: Breaking a compound down into simpler substances using heat — the heat provides the energy needed to break the bonds.
The process by which plants use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen — an endothermic reaction that stores energy in chemical bonds.

student_glossary.definition: The amount of energy stored in a bond between atoms. Breaking bonds uses energy (like pulling magnets apart), and forming bonds releases energy (like magnets snapping together). Whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic depends on which is bigger.
student_glossary.example: Think of magnets: pulling them apart takes effort (breaking bonds costs energy). Letting them snap together releases energy (forming bonds releases energy). In reactions, it works the same way.
